You Didn't Die, Now What?
Online
△ EMERGENCY What do I do right now?
Your situation
Pick the most urgent problem you are facing.
Immediate action — choose one
You Are Lost
1
Stop moving immediately. Panic walking burns energy and takes you further from known locations. Sit down.
2
Control your breathing. 4 counts in, hold 4, out 4. Do this 5 times. Your brain cannot navigate when flooded with cortisol.
3
Assess what you know. Last known position, direction travelled, time elapsed, terrain features. Say it out loud.
4
Look for high ground. A ridge or hill gives you a view of the landscape. Identify a water feature — follow it downhill if rescue is likely.
5
Stay put if rescue is expected. Searchers return to the last known point. Moving makes you harder to find. Only move with purpose and a destination.
6
Mark your location. Stamp SOS, an X, or an arrow in the ground, snow, or sand. 3 of anything is the universal distress signal.
Critical rule
Do not travel at night unless you are in immediate life-threatening danger. More injuries happen in the first 2 hours after dark than any other time.
Emergency Shelter
1
Find wind protection first. A large tree, boulder, embankment, or cliff face. Wind chill kills faster than temperature alone.
2
Insulate from the ground. Ground conducts heat away 25× faster than air. Pile dry leaves, bark, pine needles — at least 10cm thick before you lie down.
3
Smallest space possible. Your body heat warms the air around you. A small shelter retains heat; a large shelter loses it. Think coffin-sized, not tent-sized.
4
Debris hut if no materials available. Lean branches against a low ridge-pole, layer debris like shingles from ground up, pile more debris on top than you think you need.
5
Block the entrance. Your pack, a pile of debris, or layered branches. Draughts destroy insulation value completely.
Critical rule
Shelter takes priority over water and food in most survival situations. Hypothermia kills in hours. Dehydration takes days. Build shelter first.
Emergency Water
1
Collect before you purify. Rain, morning dew on leaves, snow, moving water. Collect into any container you have, even a bag or clothing.
2
Boiling is the most reliable method. 1 minute at a rolling boil kills all biological threats. 3 minutes at altitude above 2000m.
3
Unscented household bleach (if available). 8 drops per litre of clear water, 16 drops if cloudy. Wait 30 minutes before drinking.
4
Filter before purifying. Push water through layered cloth, charcoal from a fire, and sand to remove sediment. This improves both taste and purification effectiveness.
5
Collect dew at dawn. Tie absorbent cloth to your ankles and walk through vegetation. Wring it out. In some environments this yields over a litre per hour.
Critical rule
Do not drink urine, seawater, or alcohol — all accelerate dehydration. Do not eat if you have no water — digestion requires water and worsens your state.
Signal for Rescue
1
Stay at or near your last known location. Rescuers return to the last place you were seen. Moving makes every search longer.
2
Three is the universal distress signal. Three whistle blasts, three fires in a triangle, three shots, three of anything. Pause, then repeat.
3
Signal mirror or reflective surface. Visible up to 16km in sunlight. Aim at aircraft or distant ridgelines. Flash at any sound you hear.
4
Ground-to-air signals. Stamp SOS or an X in an open clearing — 3m+ per letter. Use rocks, branches, dark material — contrast matters more than size.
5
Signal fire with smoke. Green leaves, rubber, or damp material on a hot fire creates dense smoke visible for many kilometres. Best on open high ground.
Critical rule
If you have a phone, conserve battery — do not stream or browse. Send a single text with your GPS coordinates to multiple contacts. SMS often gets through when calls fail.
Injury — First Response
1
Control severe bleeding first. Direct pressure with the cleanest material available. Press hard and do not lift — lifting restarts the clotting. Hold for at least 10 minutes.
2
Tourniquet for limb bleeding that won't stop. Apply 5–8cm above the wound, tight enough to stop bleeding. Note the time applied. Do not remove in the field.
3
Suspected fracture — immobilise, do not relocate. Splint with straight sticks and cloth in the position found. Check circulation (colour, sensation, pulse) below the injury.
4
Hypothermia — gradual warming only. Remove wet clothing, insulate from ground and air, apply heat to core (armpits, groin, neck). No alcohol. No vigorous rubbing.
5
Keep the casualty still and warm. Shock follows major injury. Lay them flat, elevate legs if no spinal injury, insulate, and talk to them calmly.
Critical rule
Your priority order is: stop life-threatening bleeding → maintain airway → treat for shock → evacuate. Do not skip steps. A calm rescuer saves more lives than a fast one.
Emergency Fire Starting
1
Collect tinder before you try. The finest, driest material you can find — birch bark, dry grass, dead pine needles, frayed cloth. Have a double fistful before striking a single spark.
2
Protect your fire lay from wind and damp ground. Kneel over it as a windbreak. Build on a platform of dry bark or sticks. Wind kills flames before they establish.
3
Flint + steel (or ferro rod). Strike into a tinder bundle held in a cupped hand. A spark needs to land on the finest, driest part. Blow gently once it catches.
4
Bow drill if no ignition tools. Dry softwood (cedar, willow, cottonwood) for board and spindle. Consistent pressure and fast strokes produce an ember in a dust pile — transfer it to a tinder bundle immediately.
5
Build up gradually. Tinder → pencil-thin sticks → thumb-thick sticks → wrist-thick fuel. Adding large fuel too early smothers a young fire. Patience now saves you from starting over.
Critical rule
Wet wood can still burn once a fire is established — dry it beside the flame first. Never leave a fire unattended in the wind. A wildfire is a worse emergency than the one you're already in.
